source.title: Supernova: Achieving More with Less in Transformer Architectures

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses and cites scaling laws, but does not test any listed version: it reports no controlled loss sweep over parameter count, tokens, or compute, no small-to-large loss extrapolation, and no compute-optimal allocation sweep.
record.gate_note: The paper calls its single-model training-loss progression a predictable scaling-law pattern and gives an L(N,D) formula, but reports only one parameter/token setting, not a scaling result across settings. It also compares aggregate benchmark scores and training-token counts across models; those comparisons do not measure held-out cross-entropy scaling or compute-optimal allocation. The stated GQA quality comparison is not a loss measurement.
record.test_reason: The paper builds and evaluates a single 650M model and compares its benchmark averages with other models that differ in architecture, data and training. It reports no loss sweep over parameters, tokens or compute, no extrapolation, no allocation sweep and no controlled shape ablation. Its claim to 'challenge' scaling laws is argued from uncontrolled cross-model benchmark comparisons, not from any scaling measurement. Its L(N,D) formula is stated for one (N,D) point only, with no fit shown.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim Supernova reaches about 90% of 1B-model performance with 35% fewer parameters and 100B tokens. They say this challenges conventional scaling laws: data quality and architectural efficiency can substitute for scale. They also stress the reduced training and inference cost.
record.recipe_differences: No scaling-law method is applied; the paper reports a single model and cross-model benchmark comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Supernova (650M parameters, 100B tokens) has a benchmark average of 43.10. Larger or longer-trained comparators score 44.88–47.73.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Uncontrolled cross-model benchmark comparisons of a compact model trained on curated data versus larger models; this does not isolate scale effects.

record.problems: The comparisons use different models, datasets, and training setups, so they do not isolate parameter or token effects. The loss formula is reported for only one parameter/token setting, and no uncertainty estimates are given for the aggregate comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3's individual benchmark scores are not extracted separately: they are task-specific scores, while the aggregate comparison in Table 6 is the reported result directly tied to training-token totals. The single-run training-loss values and formula are noted in gate_note but do not test any listed version.

untested.parts: No held-out loss across parameter, token or compute sweeps. Only a single run's training loss is given (final 2.14).
No fit on small runs and no prediction of larger runs.
No depth or width ablation. The GQA-vs-MHA claim ('within 1-2%') is asserted without data or a loss measure.
No other modality or training regime is tested.
Benchmark scores come from different models with confounded data and architecture. Scale or loss is not varied in a controlled way.
No comparison of fitting choices. The L(N,D) coefficients are stated without describing how they were fitted.

record.verdict_notes: There are internal inconsistencies: the training-efficiency section says 1,000,000 training steps but also 14 days for 100,000 steps. The table average is 43.09 against 43.10 in the text. The scaling-law formula is presented for one (N,D) pair, with no fitted data shown. The claims against scaling laws are rhetorical and not tested.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute, and no test across several orders of magnitude.
No fit on smaller runs or prediction of substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token growth trends.
The paper states that GQA benchmark quality is within 1–2% of equivalent full-MHA configurations, but it does not report a loss comparison testing the version.
No tests of the loss law in other modalities or training regimes.
Benchmark results are reported across models, but there is no test of predictable downstream improvement with scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents or optimal splits across fitting choices, and no evidence of curve bending away from a fitted law.
